title: Story to Difference
context: Grade 4, and the method is finished by now, so this topic is about getting from a sentence to a working. An adult sees word problems. What is actually being separated out is two decisions that usually happen silently and at the same time: what is being asked, and which of the printed numbers answer it. The chapter says outright that a question may print more than it needs, and it asks for two step questions where doing the right two steps in the wrong order gives a wrong answer that looks worked.

writeup.why: Turn a question told in sentences into a subtraction, using only the numbers that answer what was actually asked.
writeup.look: A short question across the top with every number liftable, a row of question cards under it, and an empty column mat waiting below.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Story to Difference' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many numbers have come down onto the mat against how many the question needs, two numbers side by side in ink, with the words of the chosen question card printed small underneath them; on the second phase it carries the numbers that have been turned down as well, and on the fourth it marks which of the two steps is being worked. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The problem board is 1086 by 130 at 64,202, the sentences set large on the paper colour with every number in them drawn as a card 130 by 52 standing proud of its line; a card lifted out leaves a ruled dash in the gap so the sentence still reads, and a card pushed back settles into the dash and fills it. The shrink strip is 1086 by 56 at 64,340, drawn shut until it is opened, and it reruns the same sentence shape with single digit numbers, answers itself, and prints the move it used once underneath. The question row is four cards 260 by 48 at 64,404, at 340,404, at 616,404 and at 892,404, reading how many more, how many are left, how many to reach and how much altogether, and until one of them is picked no number card will lift at all. The column mat is 620 by 218 at 64,464: a trade strip 30 tall across its top where a lending digit is struck through once with its smaller value written above it and the ten it lent is drawn arriving in the column it went to, a heading row 34 tall of six ruled cells reading L, TTh, Th, H, T and O, the greater number 48 tall in deep blue, the number being taken away 48 tall in amber with a minus to the left of its row, a rule 4 tall, and the answer row 48 tall in green under it. A card lands on the mat by its right hand end, so a four digit number under a five digit one leaves its left hand column ruled and empty rather than closing the gap up, and a card dropped into the upper row that is smaller than the card already in the lower row will not settle: the mat holds it hovering and the two trade places under a finger. A number turned down dims where it stands to the grey this chapter keeps for a place being held open and nothing being brought, which is exactly the job that number is doing in the question, and it keeps its outline so it can still be read and pointed at. The build bay is 400 by 218 at 716,464 and stays shut and outlined until an amount is described rather than printed, when it opens with two rows of its own and the words more than standing between them, works that small subtraction in its own columns and drops the built card out of its foot with a drawn edge, so an amount that was made is told from an amount that was lifted. The step order bay takes the same rectangle on the last phase: two labelled slots one above the other with a lock on the second, which opens only when the first has been worked. The two steps may be laid down in either order, so a wrong order is seen rather than prevented. The answer sentence strip is 1086 by 40 at 64,690, blank until the answer row is full, and it then writes the finished answer back into a sentence that matches the chosen question card word for word. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever the answer has to be written, with a strip of unit words under them, kilograms, millimetres, cans, people and rupees among them, because an answer that names nothing has not answered anything yet. On the third phase the shrink strip borrows the number keys for its single digit version and hands them straight back. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the greater number on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, the answer under the rule is green, the ten lifted out of a column is vermilion and is always drawn small above the column it arrives in, a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, and a zero holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading over it before it is told by its band, and a trade is told by the strike through the lending digit and by the smaller value written above it.
writeup.finish: The card shows the question the child worked with its numbers sorted, the spare one still dimmed, and the answer written as a sentence.

phases.win: the mat holds the two numbers the right way up and the answer is written as a sentence
phases.does: picks the question card, lifts both numbers down and works the columns
phases.goal: the two amounts the question compares come down onto the mat
phases.says: Say what you are being asked for before you touch a number.
phases.check: Read me this question and then tell me what it wants without saying any of its numbers.
phases.feels: a paragraph turns into two numbers with a rule under them, and the sentences stop mattering
phases.hands: Read the question aloud, turn the page face down, and ask the child to say what is being asked for in their own words before the page is turned back over.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what does your question card say? Second rung, the phase's: which two amounts does it compare? Third rung: the question is cut to its last sentence alone with both cards showing, and the child says which of them goes on top. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: a written line is read from the left, so the order the numbers turn up in looks like the order they belong in.
wrong.move: lifts both numbers down in the order the sentences print them and sets them out that way round on the mat.
wrong.screen: the question card stays lit above the mat and the two cards are read out with what each one counts printed under it; the mat then shows both orders one under the other, and only the mat with the greater number on top has enough in its columns to pay. On the dairy's 3,929 kilograms of two kinds together, of which 1,560 kilograms is the one kind, the other comes to 2,369 kilograms, the tens fetching a ten from the hundreds on their left and those hundreds being left one less. Nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: two numbers and one mat meant adding for a whole chapter before this one, and the sentences do not shout that something is being taken away.
wrong.move: adds the two amounts because both of them count the same kind of thing.
wrong.screen: the chosen question card is reprinted large across the mat and its words are matched one at a time to what the mat would do: the card that asks how many are left and the card that asks how much altogether are stood side by side with the same two numbers under each, and only one of the two leaves the greater amount standing unchanged at the top. Both workings are left on the stage and neither is crossed out.

phases.screen: a two sentence question with two numbers in it and an empty mat
phases.soWhat: Say what is being asked, find the two amounts it is about, put the greater one on top and take the other off it.
phases.concept: Find the two numbers the question is about

phases.win: the spare number dims in its sentence, still readable, and the mat holds only two
phases.does: greys the spare number and lifts down only the two that are needed
phases.goal: a number can be printed and still have no job in the question
phases.says: One of these numbers has no job here. Which one?
phases.check: Point at the number in this question you did not use, and tell me what it was there for.
phases.feels: a number can be perfectly true and have no work at all to do in this question
phases.hands: Read a question with a pencil in hand, underline every number that answers it, draw a light box round any number that does not, and say out loud what the boxed number was there for.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does your question card ask for? Second rung, the phase's: does this number help to answer it? Third rung: the question is read back one sentence at a time with only that sentence's number liftable, so each is judged on its own. Nothing greyed is ever deleted.

wrong.why: the number is printed in the question, and until now everything printed in a question has been needed.
wrong.move: lifts the number of carriages down onto the mat along with the two counts of people.
wrong.screen: the question card stays lit and each number card is held up against it in turn with the sentence it came from printed underneath; the carriage card is the only one whose sentence says how the train is built rather than who is riding in it, and it settles back into its place in grey. The two that are left give 2,740 less 1,560, which is 1,180 people, the tens fetching a ten from the hundreds on their left. The child's answer stays in the slot beside the new one.

wrong.why: a number with no job looks like a mistake, and a mistake is a thing to take out.
wrong.move: rubs the spare number off the board so the question looks tidy.
wrong.screen: the number comes back into its sentence in grey with its outline still drawn round it, and the whole question is read through once with it standing there; grey is the colour this chapter keeps for a place being held open and nothing being brought, which is exactly what that number is doing. On the pair of towns the distance between them goes grey and the two populations give 37,648 less 26,820, which is 10,828 people, the hundreds fetching a ten from the thousands on their left.

phases.screen: a three number question where one number answers nothing
phases.soWhat: Work out what is being asked first, bring down only the numbers that answer it, and leave the spare one standing where it is.
phases.concept: Some numbers are printed to be left out

phases.win: the tiny version answers itself and the same move lands on the real numbers
phases.does: works the tiny version, names the move, then does the same to the real numbers
phases.goal: the same shape in tiny numbers shows which move is wanted
phases.says: Try the same question with tiny numbers. What did you do to those?
phases.check: What must be added to 5,621 to make 9,999? Do the tiny version out loud first and tell me what you did to it.
phases.feels: a question you could not begin becomes one you can answer out loud, and then it turns out to be the same question
phases.hands: Ask the same question with numbers small enough to answer out loud, write down what you did to those two, and then do that same thing to the real numbers on squared paper.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what would this question look like with single digit numbers? Second rung, the phase's: what did you do to those two? Third rung: the strip is opened already answered with the move printed under it, so only the copying across is left to do. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: the word standing in the sentence is the word the hands reach for, and the question plainly says that something is being added.
wrong.move: adds the two numbers because the question uses the word added.
wrong.screen: the shrink strip opens under the sentence and reruns it with single digit numbers: what must be added to four to make seven. The answer is three, and the strip writes that three as seven take four, so the move is read off a sum the child never had to work. The real sentence then takes the same move: 75,000 less 45,698 gives 29,302, and 29,302 added back to 45,698 stands at 75,000. Both the strip and the mat stay on the stage.

wrong.why: the small version feels like a different question rather than the same question wearing smaller numbers.
wrong.move: works the tiny version, gets it right, and then goes back to the real numbers and does something else.
wrong.screen: the two sentences are stood one above the other with the same words underlined in both and only the numbers different, and the move the strip used is printed once between them with an arrow running down from the strip to the mat. The strip's working stays visible while the real one runs, so the two can be read against each other without anything being cleared.

phases.screen: a reach the target question with the shrink strip open beneath it
phases.soWhat: An amount needed to reach a target is the target take away what is already there, and shrinking the numbers is how you can see that it is.
phases.concept: Shrink the question until you can see it

phases.win: the steps stand in order, the second unlocks only after the first and the answer lands
phases.does: lays the two steps out in order, then works the first one
phases.goal: the order of two steps is decided before either is worked
phases.says: Two steps here. Which one has to happen first, and why?
phases.check: One machine costs 11,050 rupees more than another and the dearer one is 35,570 rupees. Which step comes first, and what do the two cost together?
phases.feels: two steps that are both right can still come out wrong, and the only thing wrong with them was their order
phases.hands: Write the two steps down as two lines before either is worked, number them one and two, and only then pick a pencil up for the first of them.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what are your two steps, said in words? Second rung, the phase's: which of the two could you do right now with the numbers that are printed? Third rung: the bay is cut to the first step alone with the second slot locked, so only one working is open at a time. Nothing in either slot is ever marked.

wrong.why: there are two prices printed and a taking away is being asked for, so the two prices look like the two numbers to subtract.
wrong.move: takes the smaller price off the greater one, which compares the two things instead of comparing the total with what was paid.
wrong.screen: the step order bay draws both roads and labels what each one answers. Taking one price off the other answers how much dearer one thing is than the other; adding the two prices and taking the price actually paid off that total answers how much was saved. On the printer and the scanner the two prices come to 4,619 and the combined price of 4,358 leaves 261 rupees saved, the tens fetching a ten from the hundreds on their left. The other road keeps its answer too and neither is crossed out.

wrong.why: two numbers and the words more than look like an addition, and one of the two has already been printed as a price.
wrong.move: adds the two printed numbers straight away when one thing is described as costing a set amount more than another.
wrong.screen: the build bay opens beside the mat and the sentence that describes the second price underlines itself word by word: the amount printed is the dearer one, and the other is that amount less what it is dearer by. So 35,570 less 11,050 builds the cheaper machine at 24,520 with no column having to fetch anything, and only then do the two go onto the mat together and come to 60,090 rupees. The bay leaves its small working standing under the main one.

phases.screen: a question needing an addition and a subtraction, with the step order bay open
phases.soWhat: Decide the order of two steps before working either one: bought together for less wants the adding first, and priced above another wants the taking away first.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the shrink strip opens. The question standing on the board is about a number in the tens of thousands and a target in the tens of thousands, and the strip beneath it reruns the same sentence with a four where the one number was and a seven where the other was. It then answers itself while the child watches, because what must be added to four to make seven is three and everybody in the room can see that it is, and the three it writes down is written as seven take four. The move rides back up the arrow to the real sentence, which turns out to be the same question after all: the target less what is already there, so 75,000 less 45,698 is 29,302, and 45,698 and 29,302 put back together stand at 75,000. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a two sentence question is printed across the board with both of its numbers standing proud of the lines as cards, the row of question cards is face up beneath it, and the column mat below is ruled under its headings and empty with a minus already drawn to the left of its lower row. On the second the question runs to three numbers and one of them answers nothing. On the third a reach the target question stands there with the shrink strip drawn shut along its foot. On the fourth the step order bay is open beside the mat, two empty slots one above the other with a lock drawn on the second. The running count at the top left is empty and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the row of question cards gives one slow lift while the voice asks what the question is actually asking for. That lift is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: A bank of questions in sentences and tables, with the dim bay, the shrink strip and a write your own bay. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on finding the two numbers a question is about, leaving a spare one out, shrinking a question to see its shape, and ordering two steps.

observations.why: The question says which two amounts are being compared, and only those two ever go on the mat.
observations.soWhat: Choosing the numbers is a move of its own, and it happens before any taking away.
observations.observe: Picking the question card sorted the numbers before a single one had been lifted.

observations.why: Both of those shapes end as a smaller number taken off a greater one.
observations.soWhat: There are only a few shapes, and the sentences tell me which one I am holding if I read them for that.
observations.observe: A total with one part given, and two amounts compared, came down onto the same mat and were worked the same way: 3,929 less 1,560 gave 2,369, and 37,648 less 26,820 gave 10,828.

observations.why: A number is printed in a question because it is true, not because the question needs it.
observations.soWhat: I can turn a number down and still say afterwards what it was doing there.
observations.observe: The spare number stayed on the board in grey and the answer came out right without it.

observations.why: Two things bought together for less than their prices wants the total first, while one thing priced above another wants the cheaper one built first.
observations.soWhat: Two right steps in the wrong order give a wrong answer that looks properly worked.
observations.observe: One question needed adding first and taking away second, and the next one needed exactly the opposite order.

source_tool.description: A short question sits across the top of the stage in ordinary sentences, with every number in it drawn as a card that can be lifted out. Below it waits an empty column mat with a minus sign already drawn. A question row runs between them: the child says what is being asked by choosing a card reading how many more, how many are left, how many to reach, or how much altogether, and nothing can be lifted until one is chosen. A number lifted down can be pushed back up, so nothing is committed. A dim bay takes any number the question does not need and greys it where it stands, readable but out of the working, so a spare fact is visibly turned down rather than quietly deleted. A shrink strip runs the same question again with single digit numbers in place of the real ones, so a child who cannot tell whether to add or to take away can see the shape of it first. A build bay opens for the questions that describe an amount instead of printing it, works that amount out in its own small working and sends it down as a new card, and it holds two steps in order with the first one locked until it is done. The answer is written back into a sentence at the end.
source_tool.art_direction: Sentences above an empty column mat / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, bundles of ten that untie themselves, a rule between the number taken away and the answer, and a number line strip for the rounding work.

A subtraction is always shown with its columns visible: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the greater number on top, the two numbers aligned by their right ends, the minus sign to the left of the lower row, and a horizontal rule between that row and the answer. A bare line of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach taking away.

A trade is always drawn as both of its halves. The lending column keeps its digit, struck through once, with its new and smaller value written small above it, and the ten it lent is drawn arriving in the column on its right. A short arrow runs from the lending column to the receiving one, left to right, never the other way.

A check by addition is drawn under the subtraction it tests, and the total it comes to is set beside the number the working started from, so the two can be read against each other without anything being cleared.
Where tokens or bundles stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The greater number on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, and the answer under the rule is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The ten lifted out of the column on the left is vermilion, and a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, so the two halves of one trade are told apart at a glance. A zero holding a place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a lending column is told apart by the strike through its digit and by the smaller digit written above it before it is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read it again, one sentence at a time, and keep your question card showing.
voice.onNext: A new question. Say what it wants before you lift a number.
voice.opening: Read it right through. What is the question actually asking for?
voice.onFinish: Every sentence turned into a taking away, and the numbers with no job are still standing.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Sentences, tables, described amounts, and a bay for writing your own.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

placement.where: After two questions in sentences have been done on paper and at least one has gone wrong for the right reason. The tool is what makes the choosing of the numbers a move on the stage rather than something that happens invisibly.

answer_key.rule: Say what is being asked before touching a number. Then lift down only the numbers that answer it and grey the rest where they stand. A total and one part means taking the part off the total. Two amounts compared means taking the smaller off the greater. An amount needed to reach a target means taking the smaller off the target. If you cannot tell which, run the same question with tiny numbers and copy the move. Where two steps are needed, decide their order before working either: two things bought together for less than their prices means adding first and taking away after, while one thing priced above another means taking away first and adding after. Write the answer back into a sentence.
answer_key.wrong: The question is read again one sentence at a time with the chosen question card still showing, the lifted numbers go back up into their sentences, and the shrink strip opens underneath with the same shape in tiny numbers. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.

hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The question gives a whole amount and one part of it, and asks for the rest.
So the smaller number comes off the greater: 48,250 - 26,190.
The tens cannot pay and fetch a ten from the hundreds on their left, and the answer is 22,060 L.
items.question: A tank held 48,250 L of water and 26,190 L was used. How much is left?
items.checkpoint: A total and one part means taking the part off the total.
items.misconception: Adding the two amounts, because both numbers describe the same tank.

steps: The question asks about passengers, so the number of coaches has no job here and is dimmed.
The two numbers that answer it are 3,845 and 1,672.
Taking the smaller off the greater gives 2,173 passengers.
items.answer: 2,173 passengers, and the number of coaches is not needed
items.question: A train with 24 coaches carried 3,845 passengers, and 1,672 of them were children. How many were not children?
items.checkpoint: A question may print more than it needs, and a spare number is turned down rather than used.
items.misconception: Using all three printed numbers because they are all there on the page.

steps: Try the same shape with tiny numbers: what must be added to five to make nine?
Four, and four is nine take five, so the move is to take the smaller number off the target.
items.question: What should be added to 52,640 to make it 90,000?
items.checkpoint: An amount needed to reach a target is the target take the amount you have.
items.misconception: Adding 52,640 and 90,000 because the question uses the word added.

steps: The two steps have to run in order, and the total of the two prices comes first.
Add them: 7,480 + 3,260 = 10,740, which is what the two would cost separately.
Then take the price actually paid off that total: 10,740 - 9,950 = 790, so Rs 790 is saved.
items.question: A table costs Rs 7,480 and a chair costs Rs 3,260. The two together are sold for Rs 9,950. How much is saved?
items.checkpoint: Two things sold together for less means adding first and taking away after.
items.misconception: Taking 3,260 off 7,480, which compares the two prices instead of comparing the total with what was paid.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A library had 18,420 books and 7,315 were lent out. How many are left on the shelves?
One town has 36,940 people and another has 21,508. How many more people has the first town?
A depot 15 km from the town ran 2,640 trips in March and 1,925 trips in April. How many more trips ran in March?
items.final_answer: 715 trips, and the distance is not needed

items.question: A hall with 500 chairs sold 24,318 tickets in a week, and 11,207 of them were used on the first day. How many were used later?
items.final_answer: 13,111 tickets, and the number of chairs is not needed

items.question: What should be added to 14,672 to make it 30,000?
A builder needs 40,000 bricks and already has 27,516. How many more must be bought?
A fridge costs Rs 24,350, which is Rs 6,480 more than a washing machine. What do the two cost together?
items.final_answer: Rs 42,220, because the washing machine costs Rs 17,870

items.question: An account held Rs 21,308. After a payment came in the balance was Rs 68,908, and Rs 34,500 was then spent. Find the payment and the balance at the end.
items.final_answer: The payment was Rs 47,600 and the balance at the end is Rs 34,408

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: states what is being asked before any number can move
takes a number out of its sentence and down onto the mat
returns a number to its sentence, so nothing is committed
greys a number the question does not need while leaving it readable
runs the same question again with single digit numbers
works out an amount that is described rather than printed
holds two steps in order and locks the second until the first is done
writes the finished answer back into a sentence

teaching_notes: Make the question card a real step and do not let anybody past it. A child who has said out loud what is being asked has already half sorted the numbers, and a child who has not will work with whatever is printed. Keep a spare number dimmed rather than deleted. The point is not that it disappears but that it was looked at and turned down, and a child who can say why it was turned down is doing the actual work of the topic. The shrink strip is the chapter's own idea and it is worth using out loud: what must be added to four to make seven is three, and three is seven take four, so the same move works whatever the size of the numbers. Two step questions deserve the most time, because the two shapes pull in opposite directions. Two things bought together for less than their prices needs adding first and taking away after; one thing priced above another needs taking away first and adding after. Have the two steps written down in order before either is worked, and finish every question with the answer read back as a sentence, because a number with no sentence round it has not yet answered anything. The two houses on the opening page belong to this family as well.
generation_prompt: Build a word question tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A short question in ordinary sentences sits across the top with every number in it drawn as a liftable card, and an empty ruled column mat waits below with a minus sign already drawn to the left of its lower row. A question row of cards between them reads how many more, how many are left, how many to reach and how much altogether, and one must be chosen before any number can be lifted. Numbers drag down to the mat and push back up again. A dim bay greys a number in place, keeping it fully readable rather than removing it, and a dimmed number cannot be dragged. A shrink strip opens beneath the question and reruns the same sentence shape with single digit numbers, answering itself so the move can be copied. A build bay works out an amount that is described rather than printed and sends the result down as a new card. A step order bay holds two steps as labelled slots, refuses to unlock the second until the first has been worked, and accepts the two in either order so a wrong order can be seen rather than prevented. An answer sentence control writes the finished answer back into a sentence that matches the question card. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Read the question and pick the card that says what it is asking. Lift down only the numbers that answer it. Grey out any number with no job. If you cannot tell what to do, open the shrink strip and try it with tiny numbers. Write your answer back as a sentence.
